findings.title: Denial cache serves stale denies and is never cleared on allow
findings.body: In Service.Check the denial cache is checked first (permDenialCache.Get) and on a hit returns Allowed:false without querying the DB, and on a DB-verified deny it does permDenialCache.Set for shortCacheTTL (30s). Nothing ever deletes that entry on grant or on a later allow. So sequence deny -> grant permission in DB (share dashboard, add role/team permission, wildcard grant) -> Check within TTL still hits the denial key (namespace+user+action+name+parent) and denies even though the DB would allow. This reintroduces the exact staleness the PR tries to fix, but in the opposite direction, and prolongs it because the fast-path prevents the DB fallback from ever running until expiry.

findings.title: DB fallback still uses stale cached folder tree
findings.body: Check falls back to getIdentityPermissions when cached scopes miss, but checkPermission/checkInheritedPermissions then calls buildFolderTree which is itself cached in folderCache for shortCacheTTL. If the resource involves a newly created folder or new parent/ancestor relationship, the fresh permission scopes will be evaluated against the old tree, Ancestors(parent) will be empty/wrong, and the check will still deny and then populate the denial cache. The fix for newly created dashboards/folders is therefore incomplete for inherited folder permissions and List results.

findings.title: Denial key uses raw subject instead of canonical UID
findings.body: permDenialKey is built from checkReq.UserUID directly from the request subject, while permCache keys are built from resolved store.UserIdentifiers.UID after GetUserIdentifiers (which maps numeric IDs to UIDs). The same user checking as user:123 vs user:uid-string gets different denial keys, so denies can be bypassed or duplicated, and anonymous/render paths are inconsistent with the permission-cache keying.
